sources.title: Shoqan Walikhanov (Q135392), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-13): English label 'Shoqan Walikhanov', description 'Kazakhstani ethnographer (1835-1865)', Kazakh label Шоқан Шыңғысұлы Уәлиханов, instance of human, born November 1835, died 10 April 1865 (an alternative October 1865 value is also recorded), citizen of the Russian Empire; no Korean label or Korean Wikipedia article. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Nick Fielding, 'Shoqan Walikhanov: Between Empire and Steppe', Qalam (Kazakhstan), 6 January 2026 (essay by the editor of Walikhanov's English-language Selected Works, read in full). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: educated at the Omsk Cadet School from 1847, studied Kyrgyz and Kazakh folklore on the 1856 Issyk-Kul expedition (copying down part of the epic Manas and writing his first essay on the Kyrgyz), travelled to Kashgar in 1858-59 disguised as a merchant and returned in April 1859 to write 'An Expedition to Kashgar: Conditions in Altyshahr', the work that made his reputation; later memoranda on Kazakh law and society, resignation from General Chernyaev's 1864 expedition over the treatment of the local population, death from tuberculosis at 29 in 1865, and the competing nationalist and anti-collaboration readings of his legacy. Quotes Dostoevsky's letter of 14 December 1856 and Thomas Winner's 1959 judgement that he was not servile and criticised Russian policy toward the Kazakhs. A sympathetic scholar's essay that also states the collaboration criticism.

Dincer Koc, 'Chokan Valikhanov'un Mancu Isgali Altindaki Alti Uygur Vilayeti'nin Idari Yapisi Uzerine Bazi Mulahazeleri' (Observations by Chokan Valikhanov on the administrative structure of the Six Uighur Provinces under Manchu occupation), Tarih Dergisi 66, Istanbul University, 2017, pp. 107-128 (Turkish; full text read). Scholarly article whose biographical section and account of the 1858-59 journey (caravan of 43 men, 101 camels and 65 horses left on 28 June 1858 with Valikhanov using the name Alimbay; Kashgar reached on 1 October 1858; stay to mid-March 1859; collection of manuscripts and coins; the German geographer Adolph Schlagintweit had been executed there a year earlier) rely on the Soviet five-volume edition of his works; also records that he left Chernyaev's army in 1864 in protest. Text extracted from a PDF with some lost diacritics.

'Chokan Valikhanov', Kazakhstan national history portal (e-history.kz, Personalities section; page read in full). Biography based on A. Margulan and the 1984 five-volume collected works: Omsk Cadet Corps teachers' praise of his memory and industry, his service as adjutant and officer for special assignments, the 1856-57 Issyk-Kul expedition (ornithological and entomological collections, herbarium, survey of the lake shore, the first scientific record of Manas), election to the Russian Geographical Society on 27 February 1857, the Kashgar journey and report, his time in St Petersburg working on maps, his 1862 candidacy for elder sultan of Atbasar, his work on judicial reform and his departure from Chernyaev's expedition with other dissatisfied officers. Official national-heritage portal, so celebratory, and not independent of the Soviet-edition tradition.

J. K. Plumtree, 'Onegin and Manas, Valikhanov and Belinsky', Bulletin of Bishkek State University 1(67), 2024 (open-access PDF read). Critical scholarly analysis of how Valikhanov transcribed and presented a Kyrgyz Manas performance in 1856: he valued oral epics as historical and cultural records and compared them to Homer, but in his Russian summary shifted Islamic elements toward a pre-Islamic setting, left out the performer's name, and framed the narration through Russian literary criticism, possibly steering the poet by asking about the subject in advance; the transcription itself was lost for nearly a hundred years. Independent of the biographical tradition and a counter-voice on his methods.

Chokan Valikhanov, 'On the Road to Kashgar: In a Kyrgyz Aul' (English translation of excerpts from his 'Essays on Zungaria', written in St Petersburg in 1860 and printed in the Notes of the Russian Geographical Society in 1861), as published on the Cartographer Substack (page read). His own account: joined a Kokandi caravan disguised as a merchant and passed as a relative of the caravan leader; recorded Kyrgyz dwellings, hospitality, food, courtship games and mixed Islamic and shamanic practice, compared with his 1856 visit and Kazakh custom; treated rumours sceptically; declined to describe the authorities' interrogations. Self-report, used only for how he wrote and observed, not for claims about his character.

Shoqan Walikhanov, English Wikipedia (read for orientation and cross-checking dates only: the caravan of 43 men, 101 camels and 65 horses of 28 June 1858, the 1861 illness, the 1864 assignment to Chernyaev and his last months at Sultan Tezek's aul). Not used as support for any row.

curiosity.rationale: [src_wali_fielding, src_wali_ehistory, src_wali_koc, src_wali_plumtree, src_wali_essays | 1847-1865 | scholar's essay, national history portal, journal article, critical analysis, own account] As a cadet he read English literature and showed early interest in Kazakh culture, Eastern philosophy and languages (Fielding); on the 1856 Issyk-Kul expedition he compiled bird and insect collections and a herbarium and recorded folklore, copying down part of Manas (national portal, Koc); at Kashgar he gathered local manuscripts and coins and sought out merchants, officials and poets (Koc); he wrote on shamanism, law, history of the Kazakh khans and Buddhism (Fielding); and his own text records dwellings, food, games and rites in detail. Plumtree's study shows his sustained interest in oral epic. CONCENTRATION CORRECTION (agent): lowered from 80 / 0.66 (documented) to 74 / 0.58 (strong_inference) because the biographical sources share the Soviet five-volume tradition and only Plumtree's analysis and his own essay stand outside it. RUBRIC_CORRECTION (Roster67 lead review): 74@0.58 -> 72@0.54. biographical sources follow the Soviet five-volume tradition and his own 1860 essay; only one independent critical family.

risk_tolerance.rationale: [src_wali_koc, src_wali_fielding, src_wali_essays | 1858-1859 | journal article, scholar's essay, own account] He travelled to Kashgar in 1858-59 under a false merchant identity and name (Alimbay), in a region just emerging from a revolt, a year after the German geographer Adolph Schlagintweit had been executed there (Koc); Fielding calls it a year-long undercover expedition in one of the most remote Qing outposts, and his own text shows him declining to describe the interrogations of the authorities. The mission was proposed by Semyonov and ordered by the governor-general rather than chosen by him alone, and he was young and well supported, so the lean is moderate. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 76 / 0.58 to 68 / 0.5 because it rests on one ordered mission, described by sources that share a tradition, and the sources do not show how he himself weighed the danger.

adaptability.rationale: [src_wali_koc, src_wali_essays, src_wali_fielding | 1858-1861 | journal article, own account, scholar's essay] He passed as a Kokandi merchant's relative for months among Uighur and Kokandi traders, moving between steppe, Kyrgyz and Qing-Turkestan settings (Koc, his own text), and later worked in the Russian capital's map office and learned societies while remaining, in Fielding's account, an outsider there. The adaptation is documented in one episode and in his education across two cultures. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 72 / 0.55 (strong_inference) to 66 / 0.48 (inference) because the best-documented instance is the single disguise episode and the later claims are Fielding's characterisation.

independent_thinking.rationale: [src_wali_fielding, src_wali_koc, src_wali_ehistory | 1862-1864 | scholar's essay, journal article, national history portal] In 1864 he joined General Chernyaev's southward expedition but, according to Fielding and Koc, left the army in protest at the treatment of the local population (the portal says he returned with a group of dissatisfied officers); Fielding quoting Winner says he wrote memoranda criticising Russian policy toward the Kazakhs and favoured a more egalitarian approach than the tribal hierarchy, and he stood for the post of elder sultan in 1862. Koc adds that he first took part in the Russian capture of the Aulie-Ata fortress before leaving, so the protest followed participation. CONCENTRATION CORRECTION (agent): lowered from 74 / 0.6 to 66 / 0.5 because the three sources describe the same 1864 episode from one biographical tradition and the memoranda come through a single quotation.

detail_orientation.rationale: [src_wali_fielding, src_wali_koc, src_wali_essays | 1859-1860 | scholar's essay, journal article, own account] Fielding calls the Kashgar report short, packed with reliable information from climate and flora to topography; Koc reports its detailed description of Qing administrative titles and measures; his own essay records everyday detail and treats rumours sceptically. The evidence is the quality of his reports, not a documented working routine. CONCENTRATION CORRECTION (agent): lowered from 68 / 0.52 (strong_inference) to 60 / 0.44 (inference) because the claim comes from admiring descriptions of one output and Plumtree's study of his Manas work shows he also altered and omitted details.

cross_domain_range.rationale: [src_wali_fielding, src_wali_ehistory, src_wali_koc | 1856-1864 | scholar's essay, national history portal, journal article] He worked in ethnography and folklore (Manas, Kazakh epics), history and genealogy of the khans, religion (shamanism, Islam in the steppe, history of Buddhism), geography and natural history (collections and herbarium, survey of Issyk-Kul), cartography (maps of Central Asia for the General Staff), Qing administration and Kazakh customary law. Many of the fields served one programme of describing Central Asia for the Russian state and for his own people. CONCENTRATION CORRECTION (agent): lowered from 74 / 0.58 to 68 / 0.5 because the list comes mostly from one biographical tradition and the fields overlap.

proactive_agency.rationale: [src_wali_ehistory, src_wali_fielding | 1862-1864 | national history portal, scholar's essay] He stood in the local election for elder sultan of Atbasar in 1862 (Fielding says corrupt officials thwarted him; the portal says he aimed to overcome backwardness and lawlessness), then worked on the legal commission and on judicial reform of the steppe. Much of his other work was assigned by superiors. CONCENTRATION CORRECTION (agent): lowered from 66 / 0.5 to 60 / 0.44 (strong_inference to inference) because the self-started actions are only the election bid and the later reform work, thinly sourced and partly government commissioned.

portrait.source: Left half of the Semipalatinsk double portrait of Fyodor Dostoevsky (right) and Shokan Walikhanov (left), a studio photograph by Solomon (Shleima) A. Leibin made in 1858 or 1859 (the V. I. Dahl State Museum of the History of Russian Literature curator P. E. Fokin dates it to 1859). Cropped from the 800 x 1016 Wikimedia Commons scan of the full print (Commons file 'Valikhanov and Dostoyevsky (Leibin, 1850s).jpg', source given as fedordostoevsky.ru photo archive); crop 410 x 540, not resized and not upscaled. Holder records (Fokin 2020): the Dahl museum (GMIRLI) holds the print cut into two fragments, Walikhanov's being KP 35716/135 (retouched, with the dagger painted into a cane), a re-shoot KU 11043, and the full print is in the Pushkin House (IRLI) collection; this unretouched copy shows the dagger.
portrait.license: Public domain: studio photograph made in the Russian Empire in 1858-1859 by a photographer active in the 1850s; copyright long expired in Russia (author's life plus 70 years) and the work is public domain in the United States as published before 1931
portrait.attribution: Solomon (Shleima) A. Leibin, Semipalatinsk, 1858 or 1859; copy reproduced via Wikimedia Commons; originals in the V. I. Dahl State Museum of the History of Russian Literature and the Pushkin House (Moscow and St Petersburg)
portrait.creator: Solomon (Shleima) A. Leibin

provenance.notes: portrait_preflight: PLAUSIBLE (lead) / SUCCEEDED with a REPLACEMENT, LEAD DID NOT SURVIVE: the lead Commons file 'Russian scientist and traveller Shokan Valikhanov during his visit in Saint-Petersburg in 1860.jpg' (600x800, credit 'I. A. Kordovskiy (?)', Commons tags 'Images with poor sources' and 'PD-old missing SDC copyright status', source only 'Russian archival photograph') was checked against its underlying book: it is the frontispiece plate of the 1904 Russian Geographical Society edition of his Works (Notes of the IRGO, ethnography section, vol. XXIX; Commons PDF of the National Library of Kazakhstan / Russian State Library scan, page 4), and the printed credit 'Fototipiya I. A. Kordovskago, SPb., Sadovaya 98' names the 1904 phototype printer, not the photographer; the date 1860 and the underlying photograph are not documented in the plate, and the signature facsimile is not legible, so identity and provenance would rest on frontispiece position alone. It was dropped. FINAL: studio photograph by Solomon (Shleima) A. Leibin, Semipalatinsk, 1858 or 1859, double portrait with Dostoevsky, cropped to Walikhanov (left). HOLDER RECORDS (read in P. E. Fokin, 'Four portraits without retouching', Neizvestnyi Dostoevskii 2020 no. 3, by a curator of the Dahl State Museum of the History of Russian Literature, GMIRLI): the museum holds the print as two fragments (Dostoevsky KP 35714/398, Walikhanov KP 35716/135, retouched, dagger painted over as a cane, trimmed), a re-shoot KU 11043, from the Dostoevsky Museum and earlier the Museum of Dostoevsky's Memory (nos. 3105 and 3326a); the full print is in the Pushkin House (IRLI) collection; Fokin dates it to 1859, tradition says 1858; the Commons scan used here shows the dagger, so it is an unretouched print. No holder reuse statement was found (neither museum's item page was opened); rights rest on age. SITTER IDENTITY: confirmed by (a) the back inscription by Anna Dostoevskaya on the museum print ('taken on one portrait with his friend Valikhanov'), (b) Dostoevsky's letter to Wrangel of 31 October 1859 (read in Fokin) saying he gave Valikhanov a little dagger, which the left sitter holds, (c) Kapustina's 1862 letter mentioning a portrait of Dostoevsky with Valikhanov, and (d) the shaved head matching his Kashgar-journey appearance (NewTimes.kz). Visual cross-check against the 1904 frontispiece is consistent. CAVEATS: image is a crop (410x540, low resolution but not upscaled), scan from Commons not from the holder; photographer attribution rests on tradition and Fokin (no signature seen). QID VERIFIED LIVE 2026-11-13 Q135392 (human, born Nov 1835, died 10 April 1865). REGION central_asia, nationality KZ (Wikidata says Russian Empire citizen), ERA 19th_century. KOREAN NAME: Wikidata and Wikipedia carry no Korean label, so 초칸 발리하노프 is a standard transliteration from the Russian form Чокан Валиханов chosen by the agent: lead should confirm. ZERO POLITICS: only exploration, ethnography, scholarship and conduct are scored; his Russian military service, intelligence-gathering role on the Kashgar mission and role in the 1864 Chernyaev expedition are context, not scored as politics; the nationalist and collaboration debates are context. ATTRIBUTION: attributable (died at 29; sparse 7-row profile by design; evidence base thin and mostly one biographical tradition). NOT READ / BLOCKED: Kreutzmann 'On the road to Kashgar' (Brill, 403), Britannica (403), Futrell 1979 Dostoevsky and Islam (not retrieved), the 2025 Russian journal article on the Kashgar materials (PDF text unreadable), the Selected Works edited by Fielding (book), fedordostoevsky.ru (connection refused), central-asia.guide and Tengrinews (read, thin, not cited).
